nōmen, nōminis n.

noun, third declension

a noun

Also a name; in the grammarians a noun, adjectives included. A proper noun is nōmen proprium, a common noun nōmen appellātīvum (Traupman 220, 248).

Other words

  • vocābulum, vocābulī n. — a noun, a common noun

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Varr. LL 8.11: ōrātiōnis duās partēs esse dīcit, vocābula et verba (Lewis & Short); Quint. 1.4.20; Traupman 245, 247; Traupman 295

    Varro’s word for the noun beside the verb; some grammarians kept nōmen for proper names and vocābulum for common nouns (Quint. 1.4.20).

  • appellātiō, appellātiōnis f. — a common noun

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Quint. 1.4.20; Traupman 245

    Quintilian treats it, with vocābulum, as a kind of nōmen.

  • nōmen substantīvum — a noun, as opposed to an adjective

    also used · Renaissance · M-O s.v. parts of speech: noun, after Vives

    The later grammars’ term, which sets nouns apart from adjectives; substantīvus is late Latin (Lewis & Short).

  • nōmen appellātīvum — a common noun

    also used · post-classical · Charis. p. 126 P.; Prisc. (Lewis & Short s.v. appellātīvus); Traupman 294

Examples

  • veterēs enim … verba modo et nōmina et convīnctiōnēs trādidērunt; vidēlicet quod in verbīs vim sermōnis, in nōminibus māteriam (quia alterum est quod loquimur, alterum dē quō loquimur) … esse jūdicāvērunt

    For the ancients handed down only verbs, nouns and conjunctions: they judged, that is, that the force of speech lies in the verbs and its matter in the nouns (since the one is what we say, the other what we speak about)Quint. 1.4.18

  • proprium nōmen (ut “Hector”)

    a proper noun (as “Hector”)Traupman 366

  • appellātīvum nōmen (ut “homō”)

    a common noun (as “homō”, man)Traupman 366
